annotations.text:
Three directions, each now at phone size (top row) and full desktop width (below).

Built from photographs of the city rather than from architectural theory. Same content everywhere — same shuls, same times, same honest-unknown row — so this is a comparison of visual language.

Flip the Sunset toggle on any artboard.

What the extra width earned, per direction:

Photographic — the image now does two jobs at two scales: a scrimmed panoramic wash behind the masthead, and a crisp unscaled panel where the map placeholder used to be.

Night City — the gradient has room to actually gradate, plus a flat skyline silhouette and a night map with glowing pins.

Day Sea — a real horizon line, and the hero card overlaps the band edge with one curved corner: a balcony breaking a flat facade.

The photograph is real — Tel Aviv at blue hour by Martin Furtschegger, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons. Self-hosted, resized to 39KB, credited in the artboard as the licence requires.

Worth weighing: one photograph cannot represent 484 synagogues. Shipping this means either per-shul photography or a rotating set of city shots.
Kept for the record. All five were rejected as not looking like Tel Aviv — the palette is a desaturated version of the real thing.
